sections.d: อ่านบทความแล้วตอบคำถาม 9 ข้อ (ข้อ 13–21)

p.t: Salt and the Shape of Trade
x: It is difficult now to see salt as anything but the cheapest item in the kitchen, but for most of recorded history it was a strategic commodity. The reason is biological: human beings need a regular supply of sodium and cannot store it, and before refrigeration salt was also the only reliable way to keep meat and fish edible through a winter or a long voyage. Communities that had no local source therefore had to obtain salt from somewhere, every year, without exception. Few other goods combine such steady demand with such uneven supply, and that combination is what turned salt into a maker of roads.

Where salt could be produced, geography decided the method. Coastal societies with hot dry summers evaporated sea water in shallow ponds, a process that needs sunshine and wind rather than fuel and could therefore be expanded cheaply. Inland producers either mined rock salt, which required capital and skilled labour, or boiled brine from springs, which consumed enormous quantities of wood; several regions of Europe were deforested around their brine works long before industrial times. These differences in cost meant that the same substance arrived in a market town at prices that could differ by a factor of ten depending on its origin.

Because demand was inelastic, salt was an almost ideal object of taxation, and governments across Eurasia understood this. A tax that citizens cannot avoid by consuming less is attractive to a treasury and infuriating to everyone else, and salt duties produced smuggling on a scale that occasionally required armies. The French gabelle became one of the most detested features of the old regime, partly because rates varied so sharply between neighbouring provinces that carrying a sack across a boundary could be more profitable than a week's wages. Historians of the period treat the salt routes as a map of both legal trade and its shadow.

How far salt actually determined the location of towns is debated. The traditional account, popular in the nineteenth century, presented major routes as having been laid down by the salt trade and everything else as following. More recent work is cooler. Salt was rarely the only cargo on any route, and in many cases the road existed first and salt simply became the good that made it pay. What is not disputed is the pattern left behind: place names, medieval toll charters and the courses of certain old roads still record where the sacks were carried, even in regions where nobody has produced salt for two hundred years.

sections.d: อ่านบทความแล้วตอบคำถาม 9 ข้อ (ข้อ 22–30)

p.t: The Puzzle of the Domesticated Dog
x: Every dog alive today descends from the grey wolf, and yet no living wolf population matches the genetic signature of the earliest dogs. The animals that became dogs belonged to a wolf lineage that has since disappeared, which is one reason the story has proved so hard to reconstruct. Bones from sites in Europe and Siberia show animals with shortened snouts and crowded teeth by around fifteen thousand years ago, and possibly considerably earlier; the disagreement among specialists is not about whether domestication happened before farming, which is now generally accepted, but about how much before.

The older explanation was deliberate adoption. Hunters, it was said, took wolf cubs, raised them, and bred the tamest, gaining an ally for the hunt. The difficulty is practical. Hand-rearing a wolf is demanding even for modern keepers with fences and veterinary support, and a mobile group with a limited food surplus is an unlikely place to attempt it repeatedly over the many generations that visible change requires. The alternative account inverts the initiative. Human camps produced waste, waste attracted wolves, and the wolves that could feed near people without fleeing or attacking ate better than those that could not. Selection, on this view, was carried out by the wolves themselves before anyone intended anything.

Support for the second account comes from an unexpected direction. In a long-running experiment begun in Siberia in 1959, silver foxes were bred for one trait only — willingness to approach a human hand. Within a few dozen generations the foxes had not merely become tame; they had developed floppy ears, curled tails, patches of white fur and shortened faces, none of which had been selected for. The finding suggests that tameness and a cluster of physical features are linked in development, so that a population under selection for boldness near humans will drift towards a dog-like appearance without anyone breeding for looks.

That elegant result has itself been questioned. Critics have pointed out that the foxes came from fur farms and were therefore already partly accustomed to people, which may have exaggerated the speed of change, and that the celebrated physical traits were recorded less systematically than the behavioural ones. The core observation survives the criticism, but its scale is uncertain, and this uncertainty matters, because the fox experiment is often presented to the public as a demonstration of how dogs appeared. It is better read as evidence that the process is possible than as a record of what actually took place beside a particular fire, in a particular winter, some fifteen thousand years ago.

The wolf lineage that became dogs no longer exists.
Wolves and dogs cannot be told apart genetically.
Early dogs left no remains in Europe.
